question: Within how many days must a Georgia broker notify GREC in writing of a change in the address of a place of business?
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-19(a) requires a broker to notify GREC in writing of a change of place-of-business address within 30 days.

question: A brokerage firm operates sales offices in two different Georgia counties. What must the firm ensure regarding each additional place of business?
choice_a: That each additional office holds its own separate GREC branch office license
choice_b: That each office is staffed exclusively by a separate qualifying broker unrelated to the main office
choice_c: That each place of business complies with applicable local business ordinances
choice_d: That each office files a duplicate copy of the firm's trust account records with GREC
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(a) requires licensees operating from more than one place of business to comply with applicable local business ordinances for each location -- Georgia does not impose a separate state branch-office licensing requirement.

question: Does Georgia law require a broker to obtain a separate 'branch office license' or satisfy a 'definite place of business' statute before opening an additional sales office?
choice_a: Yes -- a distinct branch office license must be obtained from GREC for every additional location
choice_b: Yes -- but only firms with more than 5 affiliated licensees must obtain a branch office license
choice_c: Yes -- 'definite place of business' is a defined statutory term requiring GREC pre-approval of the office address
choice_d: No -- neither term appears in O.C.G.A. Chapter 43-40 or Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. Chapter 520-1; Georgia has no codified branch-office-licensing regime
explanation: Neither 'definite place of business' nor 'branch office' appears anywhere in O.C.G.A. Chapter 43-40 or Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. Chapter 520-1. Georgia does not have a codified branch-office-licensing regime the way some other states do; multiple offices are instead governed by local-ordinance compliance and the address-change notice requirement.
source_note: Confirmed absence in O.C.G.A. Ch. 43-40 and Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. Ch. 520-1

question: A newly licensed associate broker believes Georgia requires a firm to obtain a state 'branch office license' before opening a second sales location, similar to rules in some other states. Is this belief correct, and what does Georgia actually require instead?
choice_a: The belief is incorrect; Georgia has no branch-office-license regime, and instead requires only that each additional location comply with local business ordinances
choice_b: The belief is correct; GREC issues a separate branch office license for every additional sales location
choice_c: The belief is correct, but only for firms organized as corporations rather than LLCs
choice_d: The belief is incorrect because Georgia instead requires a $500 branch registration fee paid annually to GREC
explanation: Georgia does not have a branch-office-license or 'definite place of business' regime. What Georgia actually requires for an additional place of business is compliance with local business ordinances under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(a) -- there is no separate GREC branch licensing step.
source_note: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(a); confirmed absence of a branch-office-license regime

question: When a licensee affiliates with a sponsoring brokerage firm in Georgia, what happens to that licensee's wall certificate?
choice_a: It is mailed directly to and retained by the licensee personally at all times
choice_b: It is delivered to and kept in the custody and control of the sponsoring broker
choice_c: It is destroyed and replaced solely by a GREC-issued pocket card
choice_d: It is filed permanently with the county courthouse in the firm's home county
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-11 provides that an affiliated licensee's wall certificate is delivered to and kept in the custody and control of the sponsoring broker.

question: Besides the wall certificate held by the sponsoring firm, what does GREC separately issue to each individual licensee?
choice_a: A duplicate wall certificate for personal display
choice_b: A digital-only license accessible solely through GREC's website
choice_d: Nothing further -- only the firm receives any physical or digital credential
explanation: GREC issues each individual licensee a pocket card, separate from the wall certificate that is held in the custody and control of the sponsoring broker under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-11.

question: How long is a sponsoring brokerage firm required to retain a licensee's wall certificate or a copy of that licensee's pocket card?
choice_a: Only for the first 90 days of affiliation, after which it may be discarded
choice_b: For a fixed statutory period of exactly 4 years regardless of affiliation status
choice_c: Only until the licensee's first CE renewal cycle is complete
choice_d: As long as the licensee remains affiliated with that firm
explanation: By law, a sponsoring brokerage firm must retain a licensee's wall certificate or a copy of the licensee's pocket card for as long as that licensee remains affiliated with the firm, under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-11.

question: Under Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 520-1-.09, what must appear in a firm's real estate advertisement?
choice_a: The firm's registered name and a phone number that reaches the firm
choice_b: Only the individual listing licensee's personal cell phone number
choice_c: The firm's federal tax identification number
choice_d: A GREC-issued advertisement approval stamp obtained before publication
explanation: Rule 520-1-.09(a)-(d) requires that advertisements include the firm's registered name and a phone number reaching the firm, subject only to narrow covenant/ordinance exceptions.

question: Under Rule 520-1-.09, how must the size, prominence, and frequency of the firm's name and phone number compare to that of an individual affiliated licensee in the same advertisement?
choice_a: There is no comparative requirement -- the individual licensee's name may be displayed as prominently as the licensee wishes
choice_b: The firm's name and phone number must appear in equal or greater size, prominence, and frequency than any individual licensee's name or number
choice_c: The firm's name must appear, but may be smaller than the individual licensee's name as long as it is present somewhere in the ad
choice_d: The rule requires the firm's name and number to be exactly the same font size as the licensee's, but places no requirement on frequency
explanation: Rule 520-1-.09 requires the firm's name and phone number to appear in equal or greater size, prominence, and frequency than any individual licensee's name or number in the same advertisement.

question: An affiliated licensee places a yard sign that displays the licensee's personal cell phone number in large bold lettering, with the firm's registered name printed in small text at the bottom and no firm phone number listed at all. Does this comply with Georgia's advertising rule?
choice_a: Yes -- as long as the firm's name appears anywhere on the sign, size and phone number are irrelevant
choice_b: Yes -- Georgia's advertising rule applies only to print and online ads, not yard signs
choice_c: No -- the sign must also include a phone number reaching the firm, and the firm's name/number must be equal or greater in size and prominence than the licensee's
choice_d: No, but only because yard signs require separate GREC pre-approval, unrelated to size or content
explanation: Under Rule 520-1-.09, the sign must include a phone number reaching the firm, and the firm's registered name and phone number must appear in equal or greater size, prominence, and frequency than the individual licensee's -- a sign omitting the firm's phone number and minimizing the firm's name would violate the rule.

question: Rule 520-1-.09 generally requires a firm phone number to appear in advertisements. Under what narrow circumstance might this requirement not apply?
choice_a: Whenever the advertisement is placed on a social media platform rather than in print
choice_b: Whenever the licensee has more than 10 years of experience
choice_c: The phone number requirement has no exceptions of any kind under Georgia law
choice_d: Narrow covenant or local-ordinance exceptions recognized under the rule
explanation: Rule 520-1-.09 requires ads to include a phone number reaching the firm, subject only to narrow exceptions tied to restrictive covenants or local ordinances -- it is not a blanket requirement with no exceptions, but the exceptions are narrow rather than broad.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-1, what types of business entities may a Georgia real estate firm be organized as?
choice_a: Any business entity, including but not limited to a corporation, partnership, limited liability company, or sole proprietorship
choice_b: Only a licensed professional corporation (P.C.) formed exclusively for real estate brokerage
choice_c: Only a sole proprietorship -- corporate and LLC structures are not permitted for real estate firms
choice_d: Only a general partnership with at least two licensed brokers as partners
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-1 defines 'Firm' broadly as any business entity, including but not limited to a corporation, partnership, limited liability company, or sole proprietorship -- Georgia brokers can operate under any of these structures.

question: What must a Georgia firm have in place before its affiliated members, officers, or employees can be licensed under that firm?
choice_a: A minimum of $50,000 in firm operating capital on deposit
choice_b: A qualifying broker attached to the firm
choice_c: At least three years of continuous operation under the same trade name
choice_d: A signed reciprocity agreement with the state where the firm was originally organized
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-9 shows that firms -- including nonresident corporations or LLCs -- must qualify for a broker's license before affiliated members, officers, or employees can be licensed under that firm, i.e., a firm needs a qualifying broker attached to it.

question: A broker publishes a print ad describing a listed property's square footage as substantially larger than its actual measured size, in order to attract more inquiries. What has the broker most likely violated?
choice_a: Nothing, as long as the buyer independently verifies square footage before closing
choice_b: Only a nonbinding GREC advisory guideline with no disciplinary consequence
choice_c: The statutory prohibition on misleading or inaccurate advertising
choice_d: The Real Estate Education, Research and Recovery Fund contribution requirement
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b) enumerates misleading or inaccurate advertising as a statutory unfair trade practice ground for discipline -- overstating a property's square footage to attract inquiries falls within this prohibition.

question: A licensee places a 'For Sale' sign on a property without first obtaining the owner's consent. Is this a violation of Georgia license law?
choice_a: No -- signage placement is unregulated under Georgia license law as long as the property is under a valid listing agreement
choice_b: No -- consent is only required for commercial properties, not residential
choice_c: Yes, but only if the sign lacks the firm's name and phone number
choice_d: Yes -- placing a sign without the owner's consent is an enumerated unfair trade practice
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b) enumerates improper 'for sale' signage as an unfair trade practice, specifically including placement of a sign without the owner's consent.

question: A listing expires, but the licensee leaves the 'For Sale' sign standing in the yard for 15 days afterward without removing it. What does Georgia license law say about this?
choice_a: It is an enumerated unfair trade practice to fail to remove a 'for sale' sign within 10 days of the listing's expiration
choice_b: There is no time limit for sign removal after a listing expires under Georgia license law
choice_c: The licensee has 30 days from expiration to remove the sign, matching the address-change notice period
choice_d: Sign removal timing is governed solely by county code enforcement, not GREC license law
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b) enumerates, as an unfair trade practice, failure to remove a 'for sale' sign within 10 days of a listing's expiration -- leaving the sign up for 15 days would exceed that window.

question: As a general national real estate office-management practice (not a Georgia-specific statutory figure), what is commonly recommended regarding retention of brokerage transaction files after a deal closes?
choice_a: Destroying all transaction files within 30 days of closing to minimize storage costs
choice_b: Retaining complete transaction files for a period of several years, commonly cited as around 3 to 5 years, as a risk-management best practice
choice_c: Retaining files indefinitely is legally prohibited in every U.S. state
choice_d: No retention period is ever recommended for closed transaction files in any jurisdiction
explanation: As a matter of general national practice rather than a confirmed Georgia-specific statutory figure, brokerages are commonly advised to retain closed transaction files for a period of several years (often cited around 3-5 years) for liability and audit purposes.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate office-management practice; not a Georgia-specific statutory retention period confirmed this session
